en: When I alone held
And ruled the face of the earth,
Why did I not die then?!
My falcon Manas, had you not died,
Khan Bakai would not have lived so long
And come to this pass!
May such humiliation
Never be given to a mortal!
The accursed ones have finished my days
By refusing to heed my words!
Your uncle Bakai has died
And beheld the face of the next world!”
Prince Bakai grieved;
Of Lord Manas, the gray wolf,
His death became clear only today!
“I have departed from the world;
Because the children did not heed my words,
Today Bakai has passed away!
Having let the horses be raided on the way,
How can I go to Kakan?
How can I gird my waist?
From the Kalcha who styles himself a hero—
Oh, what a cruel day!—
How can I pursue the blood-price?!
How can I strike Kakan?
How can I go to Beijing?!
From the Kalcha in Beijing,
How can I exact my vengeance?!
Accursed Bakai has died;
In his old age this Bakai
Has beheld the face of judgment!
Parted from fourteen horses,
How can I remain alive?
The land of Beijing lies six months away;
The road between is not short.
Refusing to heed my words,
My children, what you have done is not right!
Great Beijing lies seven months away;
It is no easy road to reach.
The capable youths did not heed my words;
What they have done is not right!
Bakburchun lies before you;
When we rode out to reconnoiter,
When we brought slaughter upon the Chinese,
When the heroes took their vengeance,
We turned back from our wings,
And lost the fourteen horses
That stood there like a dark mass.
How shall we go straight in and strike
Deep-rooted Beijing,
Now that we have lost our swift horses?
How shall we reach Beijing?!
When I spoke, you did not heed me;
You did not return to guard the horses,
And would not obey the words I spoke!”
Thus Khan Bakai
Reproached the warriors harshly.
Hero-sultan Bakai said this,
Uttering all manner of bitter words.
Turning back in sorrow,
Külchoro and Kanchoro
Came together from one direction,
Having lost the fourteen horses.
The companions came then,
Turning toward their prince.
The boys stood before
Bakai and the hero;
God had struck the boys,
For they had lost the fourteen horses.
Their hearts were torn,
And tears poured from their eyes:
“Our dear heroes,
We let them be raided from the Kyrmaly side,
And let the mighty swift tulpars
Be taken from that narrow place!
Here is the sovereign city;
If you would cut off our heads, here we are!
Here is the lovely upland;
Lion uncle Bakai,
If you would take my life, here I am!
Nothing at all appeared
Before these accursed eyes—
Did we drink too much water in the night
Until it rose into our eyes?!
Nothing whatsoever appeared
Before these benighted eyes—
Did we drink water in the darkness
Until God struck our sight?!
We turned back from the wings
And lost the fourteen horses!
Traveling on campaign, we ate no proper food,
But took our meal from black liquor;
We became drunk.
By failing to guard the horses on campaign,
We acted like foolish youths!
Traveling on campaign without tending the horses,
We became drunk!
Riding reconnaissance without tending the horses,
We have come to ruin!
Riding reconnaissance and sleeping too long,
We have proved worthless!
Gouge out our blinded eyes;
If your anger rises in fury,
Khans, slaughter us!”
The boys wept, their hearts torn;
In their distress,
Tears poured from their eyes.
They drew back their heads, sobbing;
The boys wailed as they wept.
Their hearts were torn,
Tears pouring from their eyes;
Grieving in sorrow,
The gray wolves could not endure it,
And their whole insides burned with fire.
“There was no broad daylight, nor even afternoon;
We companions who lost fourteen horses
Have no share of good fortune!
Had we lost the horses by day,
Had we faced the enemy openly,
Had we stood face-to-face,
What regret would we have
If we had clashed in battle?!
Had death reached us and we died,
We would have had no regret.
Enough, my hero-sultan;
If you wish, let us live.
If you are angry, my sultan,
Seize us and slaughter us!
When we lie dead,
We shall be slaves worth a dog's hide;
While we walk alive,
We are slaves worth a sheep's hide!
Our slavish worth has been revealed:
We lost the fourteen horses
When sleep closed our eyes.
If you wish, let us live!
If you do not wish it, uncle,
Seize us and slaughter us;
We were but two wretched slaves.
He who girded his waist firmly,
My hero born together with me,
Came kicking through the womb
Of my dear mother Kanykei,
Sprang straight from the loins
Of generous lion Manas.
When were we ever sons of Manas?
Could youths like us
Ever be called brave men?
We let the tulpars be taken—
Could any man be like us!”
While the boys stood grieving,
The hero rose and said:
“Do not grieve, boys, do not grieve!
For kinsmen such as you two,
An uncle like me would give his life!
My morning star in the sky,
My sable fur upon my collar!
My support when I climb upward,
My prop when I descend!
The lost horses will be found;
My two matched companions,
Tomorrow our honor will be restored.
There is no remedy in grieving over what is gone,
And no profit in regret.
Upon the swarming Chinese
We shall bring terrible slaughter,
And raid the horses
Of the red-naveled Kalmaks!
Breaking through the stones, taking their migration,
We shall crush them and take revenge;
Breaking through the desert road, taking their migration,
We shall pursue them and take revenge.
My kinsmen, boys, do not grieve!
We shall scatter the four kinds of livestock
Of the lordly Manchu,
Of the Kalmak who descended upon you!
We too shall divide
The city of Kün Jang-jun;
We shall contend
With the slave who boasts of strength!
Whose robe hem never touched the earth,
Who does not know which one
Is Almighty Allah alone—
In the camp of those bloodthirsty men,
We too shall bring splendid slaughter.
To Khan Kongurbai's city,
To precious Beijing,
We shall go and bring slaughter!
Against the people of Madangshan,
Against their chief, Khan Zuntung,
You shall see your battle
In the city of the Kakanchin!
The land you will face is Beijing;
Look at its multitudes, like black worms!
To the tent upon the riverbank,
We shall go and grapple
With the blood-drinking Kalcha hero!
The people you will fight are the Kalmaks;
Because the Kalmak raided the horses,
Is it right to despair?!
Because the Chinese raided the horses,
Should we seethe in anguish?!
Because the Kalmak took the horses
And brought us suffering,
Should we keep letting them be taken?!
If I remain alive, just watch:
I shall drive my caravan from Kerüü;
Unless I die, I shall take my revenge
Upon the Kalcha khan of the monks!
Because the Chinese took the horses,
Should we seethe in anguish?!
Does a warrior not encounter hardship?
You are children of a dark day;
Does grief not divide one's reason?!
Does a brave man who rides on patrol
Not encounter every kind of peril?!
Can grief serve as payment?
Because the Kalmak took the horses,
Should we go on grieving?!”
He spoke words of courage to the boys.
The dear hero stood towering;
The dear warrior did not stir at all.
Standing erect, he paid it no heed,
And counted the boys' grief
As less than the hem of his robe.
He fastened on his golden belt-pouch,
And radiance like moonlight touched the face
Of the gray wolf, pure-born from his father.
Your gray wolf grew wrathful,
Standing tall without distress;
He mounted Buurul and rode out,
Your dear prince looming high.
In the broad valley of Üch-Karkyra,
Unable to find the trail here,
He now turned back.
Straight across Charyn and Chara,
Your gray wolf descended
Into the Lower Charyn plain.
Nothing caught his eye;
Where the powerful weather-worker Muradyl
Had driven them away
Could not then be determined.
He searched along the mountainside;
They say he examined in turn
Ylailuu-Kyr and Aigai-Tash,
But found no trail.
He searched Kyygach-Kyr,
And followed the winding Kara-Suu
Along its course.
Unable to find the trail here,
He searched across a great distance.
They say he crossed Üch-Kaiky,
And passed through Ükürchü;
He searched down through Üch-Kapkak,
Along the flowing waters
Of the Tekes River.
